section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Wave Nature of Light
section_1.content: Briefly introduce the wave property of light (wavelength and phase). Explain that light behaves like ripples in a pond. Emphasize that 'coherence' (stable phase relationship) is the fundamental requirement for both diffraction and holography.
section_1.example: Visualizing a laser beam as a perfectly rhythmic, single-colored ocean wave compared to a messy, chaotic splash from a flashlight.

section_2.title: The Phenomenon of Diffraction
section_2.content: Explain diffraction as the 'bending' of light around obstacles or through slits. Introduce the concept of the interference pattern—a spatial map of light intensity peaks and troughs created when light waves overlap.
section_2.example: A digital animation showing water waves passing through a narrow harbor entrance and spreading out, analogous to light passing through a tiny pinhole.

section_3.title: The Holographic Recording Process
section_3.content: Break down the holographic process: 1. Reference beam (direct light) + 2. Object beam (scattered light) = Interference pattern. Explain how this pattern is 'frozen' on a film as a complex grayscale grid.
section_3.example: A 3D character (like a robotic cat) being illuminated; the interference pattern is visualized as a complex, swirling fingerprint-like map recorded on a sensor.

section_4.title: The Holographic Reconstruction
section_4.content: Explain how illuminating the recorded interference pattern with the original reference beam acts like a 'diffraction grating,' bending light to recreate the original wavefronts, effectively reconstructing the 3D object in space.
section_4.example: A holographic 'Iron Man' display: light hitting the recorded film 'bends' specifically to reconstruct the light waves that originally bounced off the hero, making him appear to float in thin air.

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Conclude by linking the two: Holography is essentially a sophisticated control of diffraction. Final takeaway: You aren't just storing a picture; you are storing the complete physical geometry of light waves.
section_5.example: Comparing a 2D photograph (a flat map) to a hologram (a time-capsule of 3D light) used in modern medical imaging and secure bank card authentication.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=20, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT, buff=0.4).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)
        self.lecture.set_opacity(0)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Columns 4-6 are preferred for primary animation objects
                x = 2.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        # Setup visual elements

        self.play(FadeIn(hologram))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color("#FF4500"))
        self.wait(2)
